rationale: A wins by a nose because it is more disciplined about what can actually be pitched now and what has to wait. Its next step says "journalist-fit-check for the margin angle" and holds the weaker retailer and product angles until proof exists; B's "three viable shapes exist. Pick one" is useful but less decisive. B also lets causal fog creep in with "store closures plus a 40% product-range cut producing" when the update only says those moves happened under the same turnaround plan.
gaps_in_A: "Allbirds shrinks its way to a first margin gain" is punchy, but "first margin gain" should be nailed to the exact fact: first quarter of gross-margin improvement under the turnaround plan.
"selling less, not selling better" is a sharp reporting question, but it needs to stay framed as a test, not a conclusion. The update does not prove what caused the margin improvement.

"The retailer betting shelf space on Allbirds' second act" cannot be pitched until the supposedly named wholesale partner is actually named and available. A admits this, but it is still the softest kept angle.
gaps_in_B: "store closures plus a 40% product-range cut producing the first quarter of gross-margin improvement" implies causation the update does not give. That is how a smart reporter catches spin in sentence two.
"Story type: category-creation" is the wrong label for the shoe angle. One new sugarcane-and-wool platform with an unverified durability claim is not category creation.

"Allbirds posts its first gross-margin gain" is looser than the supplied fact. The update says first quarter of gross-margin improvement under a turnaround plan, not necessarily Allbirds' first gross-margin gain ever.
"three viable shapes exist. Pick one" dodges the strategist's job. The data angle has the strongest supplied facts; the other two need missing proof before they deserve outreach.
